title: Homomorphism
body:
A map between two groups that respects the operation. For $\varphi: G \to G'$,

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) \quad \text{for all } a, b \in G$$

with the product on the left taken in $G$ and the one on the right in $G'$. That single equation
is the definition, and everything else is forced by it:

- $\varphi(e) = e'$
- $\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}$
- $\varphi$ sends subgroups to subgroups, and the order of $\varphi(a)$ divides the order of $a$

**It does not have to be injective or surjective.** A homomorphism is allowed to lose
information, and how much it loses is the interesting part. An [[Isomorphism]] is the special
case that loses none.

## The three examples worth memorising

| $\varphi$ | From | To | Loses |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x \mapsto x \bmod n$ | $\mathbb{Z}$ | $\mathbb{Z}_n$ | which lap you were on |
| $\sigma \mapsto \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ | $S_n$ | $\{\pm 1\}$ | everything but parity |
| $A \mapsto \det A$ | $GL_n$ | $\mathbb{R}^*$ | everything but the volume factor |

Each is a legitimate structural statement about the source. That $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$ is
exactly the claim that [[Determinant]] is a homomorphism, and it is worth reading it that way:
the multiplicativity is not a computational accident, it is the reason determinants are useful.

The same is true of parity in [[Permutation Group]]. "Even times odd is odd" is the sign map
being a homomorphism into a two-element group.

## Kernel and image

$$\ker\varphi = \{a \in G : \varphi(a) = e'\}, \qquad \operatorname{im}\varphi = \varphi(G)$$

The kernel is what collapses to nothing, and the image is what actually gets hit. Both are
subgroups, the kernel of $G$ and the image of $G'$.

**$\varphi$ is injective exactly when $\ker\varphi = \{e\}$.** So the kernel measures the failure
to be an isomorphism, and one element's worth of kernel means no failure at all. This is the same
statement as [[Kernel and Range]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]: a [[Linear Transformation]] is a
homomorphism of additive groups that also respects scaling, and "injective iff trivial kernel" is
proved there by the identical argument.

The **first isomorphism theorem** ties it together: $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$.
Quotient out exactly what the map forgot and what is left is what the map saw. The kernel's
[[Coset|cosets]] are the fibres of $\varphi$, which is why the quotient is the right object.

Kernels are precisely the normal subgroups, so the two ways of building a quotient group, from a
map or from a subgroup, produce the same list.

## Structure-preserving maps elsewhere

The pattern generalises past groups: a [[Ring]] homomorphism respects both $+$ and $\times$, and
a [[Field]] homomorphism is one of those between fields (and is automatically injective, since a
field has no proper non-zero ideals). Whenever the vault says "structure-preserving map", this is
the shape being described.
